source.title: Provable Scaling Laws for the Test-Time Compute of Large Language Models
source.authors: Yanxi Chen; Xuchen Pan; Yaliang Li; Bolin Ding; Jingren Zhou

record.file_problem: not stated; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It tests whether downstream-task accuracy changes as inference-time compute is increased, using accuracy curves and theoretical analyses rather than pretraining loss scaling.
record.gate_note: The study varies test-time candidate count and comparison compute and reports accuracy, not held-out pretraining cross-entropy as a function of parameter count, training tokens, or training compute. It does not test a compute-optimal pretraining allocation. Its accuracy results bear on V6 as test-time compute scaling; they do not establish the pretraining-loss claims in V1–V5 or V7.
record.test_reason: The paper's 'scaling laws' are about test-time compute: failure probability of its own knockout and league aggregation algorithms as candidate count N and comparisons K grow. It trains no models and varies no parameters, tokens or training compute. It measures no pretraining loss and does not relate downstream accuracy to model scale or pretraining loss. It does not cite or rely on the original sources. Every result is its own method's accuracy versus N, sometimes against majority voting, so the record's T2/V6 link is wrong: V6 concerns scale in the pretraining sense.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. More precisely: the authors prove that failure probability of the knockout algorithm decays exponentially (scaling N and K) or as a power law (scaling N with K fixed). They prove exponential decay for the league algorithm. Both rest on assumptions about generation and pairwise-comparison ability. Experiments show accuracy rising with N across Llama3.1, Qwen2.5, Mixed, GPT-4o and QwQ-32B, with gains that depend on task and backend.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies inference-time candidate generation and pairwise aggregation; it does not train models or fit pretraining-loss scaling curves.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scaling outcome varies by model backend, task category, and aggregation algorithm; the authors also report that knockout scaling eventually plateaus on the filtered subset.

fits_no_version.finding: For fixed LLMs, accuracy of pairwise-comparison aggregation (knockout/league) rises with test-time candidate count N on GPQA, MMLU-Pro-S and MATH-500. The rise varies by backend and task category and plateaus on filtered subsets. Theory gives exponential or power-law decay of failure probability in N, K under assumptions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inference-time compute scaling: task accuracy of sampling-plus-aggregation methods improves predictably (power-law/exponential failure decay) with test-time compute.

record.problems: The authors report running each algorithm only once for each model-dataset combination and provide no error bars, noting that repeated experiments would be computationally expensive. Exact values for many curves are only available in figures. Experiments cover a limited set of models and tasks, and theoretical guarantees depend on assumptions that the authors say may not always hold.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed figure-only curves for the remaining GPQA categories, MMLU-Pro-S categories, MATH-500, and league-style opponent-subsampling settings were not extracted individually. These are shown across Figures 6–19; the selected rows retain the explicit text-reported outcomes and examples of task/backend-dependent scaling.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute.
No other modalities or training regimes.
No downstream performance vs model scale or pretraining loss; only test-time candidate count for the authors' algorithms.
No fitted exponents or fitting-choice comparisons for pretraining laws.

record.verdict_notes: The term 'scaling law' here means test-time compute for a proposed inference method. It is unrelated to the Kaplan/Hoffmann pretraining laws in V1–V7. Recommend excluding the study from the claim's verdict tables. Each configuration was run once, with no error bars.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or training compute.
Whether small-run pretraining-loss fits predict much larger training runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation for pretraining.
Architecture-shape effects at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
The study tests downstream accuracy against test-time compute, not against model parameter scale or pretraining loss; it does not test predictability across a broad range of model scales.
Dependence of pretraining-loss exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices and setup.
